\section[o estágio]{o estágio — the internship, the traineeship; the stage}

\label{lesson:PT-C357-estagio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for unemployed, then the Portuguese for the unemployment.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o estágio}
\textbf{o estágio} — \textquotedblleft{}the internship, the traineeship; the stage\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Fiz um estágio de três meses num hotel.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I did a three-month internship in a hotel.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Estágio profissional} — work placement. Also a stage or phase.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{estágio} is usually traced to French \emph{stage} \textquotedblleft{}a period of training\textquotedblright{}, which EtymDB derives from Medieval Latin \emph{stagium} (EtymDB), a formation on Latin \emph{stāre} \textquotedblleft{}to stand\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o estágio}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{o estágio}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for unemployed, then the Portuguese for the unemployment, then say \emph{o estágio} again
\end{itemize}

\section[o estagiário]{o estagiário — the intern, the trainee}

\label{lesson:PT-C357-estagiario}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the unemployment, then the Portuguese for the internship.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o estagiário}
\textbf{o estagiário} — \textquotedblleft{}the intern, the trainee\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O estagiário novo aprende muito depressa.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The new intern learns very quickly.}
\end{quote}

Feminine \emph{a estagiária}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{estagiário} is built on \emph{estágio} \textquotedblleft{}internship\textquotedblright{} with \emph{-ário}; \emph{estágio} is usually traced to French \emph{stage}, from Medieval Latin \emph{stagium} (EtymDB), on \emph{stāre} \textquotedblleft{}to stand\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[o aprendiz]{o aprendiz — the apprentice}

\label{lesson:PT-C357-aprendiz}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the internship, then the Portuguese for the intern.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o aprendiz}
\textbf{o aprendiz} — \textquotedblleft{}the apprentice\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ele começou como aprendiz numa padaria.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He started as an apprentice in a bakery.}
\end{quote}

Plural \emph{os aprendizes}; close to \emph{aprender}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{aprendiz} is usually traced to Old French \emph{aprentis} \textquotedblleft{}learner\textquotedblright{}, the older form of French \emph{apprenti} (EtymDB), built on \emph{aprendre} \textquotedblleft{}to learn\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{apprehendere} \textquotedblleft{}to lay hold of, to seize\textquotedblright{}, on \emph{prehendere} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[empregar]{empregar — to employ; to use}

\label{lesson:PT-C357-empregar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the intern, then the Portuguese for the apprentice.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: empregar}
\textbf{empregar} — \textquotedblleft{}to employ; to use\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A fábrica emprega duzentas pessoas.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The factory employs two hundred people.}
\end{quote}

Also to use: \emph{empregar bem o tempo} — to use your time well.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{empregar} is inherited from Latin \emph{implicāre} \textquotedblleft{}to fold into, to involve\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB, Lewis \& Short), through Old Portuguese \emph{empregar}; the learned form of the same verb is \emph{implicar}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[a entidade patronal]{a entidade patronal — the employer}

\label{lesson:PT-C357-entidade-patronal}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the apprentice, then the Portuguese for to employ.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a entidade patronal}
\textbf{a entidade patronal} — \textquotedblleft{}the employer\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A entidade patronal tem de pagar as férias.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The employer has to pay for the holidays.}
\end{quote}

European Portuguese, formal; in speech \emph{o patrão}. In Brazil \emph{o empregador}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{entidade} is usually traced to Medieval Latin \emph{entitās}, built on \emph{ēns} \textquotedblleft{}being\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{patronal} is built on \emph{patrono}, from Latin \emph{patrōnus} \textquotedblleft{}protector, patron\textquotedblright{}, on \emph{pater} \textquotedblleft{}father\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a entidade patronal}, once more

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the apprentice, then the Portuguese for to employ, then say \emph{a entidade patronal} again
